chapterNote: For the first time the Preacher turns and addresses the reader directly, and the subject is worship. Guard your steps at God's house; come to listen, not to perform; keep your words few, for God is in heaven and you are on earth; and if you vow, pay — the mouth can put the whole body in debt. Then the chapter descends from the sanctuary to the marketplace and runs the money question to the bottom: bureaucracy shields oppression layer above layer, the lover of silver is never satisfied by silver, wealth attracts eaters as fast as it grows, and the rich man's abundance robs him of the laborer's sweet sleep. The naked-in, naked-out verdict of verse 15 is the coldest arithmetic in the book. Yet the chapter ends warm: when God gives both wealth and the power to enjoy it, that is His gift, and He keeps such a man so occupied with the joy of his heart that the vapor-days pass without brooding.

1.text: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God, and draw near to hear rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not even know that they are doing evil.
1.amp: Keep [shamar — guard] your foot [regel] when you go to the house [bayith] of God [Elohim], and be more ready to draw near [qarov] to hear [shama] than to give [natan] the sacrifice [zebach] of fools [kesil]: for they know [yada] not that they do evil [ra].
1.notes: shamar (H8104), to guard: approach worship the way a watchman approaches a post. shama (H8085) is to hear with the intent to obey, and the kesil's zebach (H2077), his sacrifice, is worship as performance — ritual so unexamined the fool cannot tell it has become sin (cf. 1 Samuel 15:22).

2.text: Do not be rash with your mouth, and do not let your heart hurry to bring a word out before God; for God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few.
2.amp: Be not rash [bahal — alarmed into haste] with your mouth [peh], and let not your heart [leb] be hasty [mahar] to utter [yatsa — bring out] any thing [dabar] before [panim] God [Elohim]: for God is in heaven [shamayim], and you upon earth [eretz]: therefore let your words [dabar] be few [meat].
2.notes: bahal (H926) is to be flustered into speaking, and mahar (H4116) to hurry: two speed-words against one slow God. The geography is the argument — heaven above, earth below — so meat (H4592), few, is the only fitting word-count for the creature's side of the conversation.

3.text: For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with a multitude of words.
3.amp: For a dream [chalom] comes [bo] through the multitude [rob] of business [inyan]; and a fool's [kesil] voice [qol] is known by multitude [rob] of words [dabar].
3.notes: The proverb pairs two overflows: too much inyan (H6045), busyness, spills over into restless dreams, and too many dabar (H1697), words, betray the kesil (H3684). Volume, in both senses, is the fool's signature.

4.text: When you vow a vow to God, do not put off paying it, for He takes no pleasure in fools. What you have vowed, pay.
4.amp: When you vow [nadar] a vow [neder] unto God [Elohim], defer [achar — delay] not to pay [shalam — complete, make good] it; for He has no pleasure [chephets] in fools [kesil]: pay [shalam] that which you have vowed.
4.notes: nadar (H5087) with its noun neder (H5088), the solemn voluntary promise, and shalam (H7999), to make complete or whole — the payment-word built on the same root as shalom. An unpaid vow is an open wound in one's peace with God (cf. Deuteronomy 23:21).

5.text: It is better not to vow at all than to vow and leave it unpaid.
5.amp: Better [tov] is it that you should not vow [nadar], than that you should vow and not pay [shalam].
5.notes: The vow was always voluntary; the payment never is. Silence before God carries no penalty, but shalam (H7999) left undone turns devotion into debt.

6.text: Do not let your mouth drag your flesh into sin, and do not stand before the messenger and plead, 'It was a mistake.' Why should God be angry at the sound of your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
6.amp: Suffer [natan — allow] not your mouth [peh] to cause your flesh [basar] to sin [chet]; neither say [amar] before [panim] the angel [malak — messenger], that it was an error: wherefore should God [Elohim] be angry [qatsaph] at your voice [qol], and destroy the work [maaseh] of your hands?
6.notes: The peh (H6310), the mouth, can indebt the whole basar (H1320), the body that must labor to pay. The malak (H4397) is the temple messenger, the priest come to collect the vow; 'it was an error' pleads the accidental-sin category (H7684, shegagah) for a promise made wide awake. qatsaph (H7107) is kindled wrath.

7.text: For in a multitude of dreams there is vapor, and in many words the same; but as for you, fear God.
7.amp: For in the multitude [rob] of dreams [chalom] and many [rabah] words [dabar] there are also divers vapors [hebel]: but fear [yare — revere, stand in awe of] thou God [Elohim].
7.notes: Dreams and word-torrents alike dissolve into hebel (H1892). Against both stands the shortest sentence in the chapter: yare (H3372) Elohim, fear God — the book's ballast, dropped here mid-voyage before it anchors the whole conclusion (cf. Ecclesiastes 12:13).

8.text: If you see the poor oppressed in a province, and justice and righteousness torn away by force, do not be astonished at the business, for one high official watches over another high official, and higher ones still are over them.
8.amp: If you see [raah] the oppression [osheq — extortion] of the poor [rush], and violent perverting of judgment [mishpat] and justice [tsedek] in a province [medinah], marvel not at the matter [chephets]: for he that is high [gaboah] is watched [shamar] by a higher [gaboah], and there be higher than they.
8.notes: osheq (H6233) is extortionate oppression, and gaboah (H1364), high, is stacked three times: the bureaucratic tower where each official shields and skims off the one below. Read from under the sun it explains corruption; read upward, the highest watcher of all still keeps shamar (H8104) over every rung.

9.text: And yet the profit of the earth is for all; even the king himself is fed from the field.
9.amp: Moreover the profit [yithron] of the earth [eretz] is for all: the king [melek] himself is served [avad] by the field [sadeh].
9.notes: yithron (H3504), the surplus-word, finally finds a home in the soil: the field's yield is the one profit everyone shares. avad (H5647), to serve: even the melek at the top of verse 8's tower eats only because a farmer works the sadeh (H7704).

10.text: Whoever loves silver will never be satisfied with silver, and whoever loves abundance is never satisfied by its increase. This also is vapor.
10.amp: He that loves [ahab] silver [keseph] shall not be satisfied [saba] with silver; nor he that loves abundance with increase: this is also vapor [hebel].
10.notes: ahab (H157), to love, aimed at keseph (H3701), money: the appetite is disordered at the object, so saba (H7646), satisfaction, never arrives — more of the wrong thing cannot fill a place shaped for something else.

11.text: When goods increase, those who eat them increase right along with them; and what good is it to the owner, except to watch it all with his eyes?
11.amp: When goods [tov] increase [rabah], they are increased that eat [akal] them: and what good is there to the owners [baal] thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes [ayin]?
11.notes: Wealth attracts eaters at the speed it grows: dependents, staff, hangers-on. The baal (H1167), the owner, ends up with a spectator's share, watching his own estate feed everyone else.

12.text: Sweet is the sleep of the working man, whether he eats little or much; but the rich man's fullness will not let him sleep at all.
12.amp: The sleep of a labouring man [avad — the one who serves and works] is sweet, whether he eat [akal] little [meat] or much [rabah]: but the abundance of the rich [ashir] will not suffer [yanach — permit, give rest to] him to sleep [yashen].
12.notes: The laborer's tired body buys what the ashir's (H6223) portfolio cannot: sweet sleep. yanach (H3240), to give rest — the very thing abundance refuses its owner, who lies awake managing what he cannot stop counting.

13.text: There is a sickening evil I have seen under the sun: riches hoarded by their owner to his own hurt.
13.amp: There is [yesh] a sore [chalah — sickening] evil [ra] which I have seen [raah] under the sun [shemesh], namely, riches kept [shamar — hoarded, guarded] for the owners [baal] thereof to their hurt [ra].
13.notes: chalah (H2470) makes the evil literally sickening, and shamar (H8104), the guarding-word from verse 1, is here turned pathological: keeping become hoarding. ra (H7451) frames the verse at both ends — the evil and the hurt are the same word.

14.text: For those riches perish in a bad venture, and the son he fathered is left with nothing at all in his hand.
14.amp: But those riches perish [abad] by evil [ra] travail [inyan — a bad business]: and he begets [yalad] a son [ben], and there is nothing in his hand.
14.notes: abad (H6), to perish and vanish: one ra inyan (H6045), one bad business venture, and the hoard is gone. The empty hand of the ben (H1121) answers chapter 2's fear about heirs with something worse — an heir with nothing left to inherit.

15.text: Naked he came from his mother's womb, and naked he will return, going out just as he came; and from all his toil he can take away nothing that his hand can carry.
15.amp: As he came forth [yatsa] of his mother's [em] womb [beten], naked shall he return [shub] to go as he came [bo], and shall take [nasa — lift, carry] nothing of his labour [amal], which he may carry away in his hand.
15.notes: The arithmetic of a lifetime: yatsa (H3318) naked, shub (H7725) naked, and nasa (H5375), the carrying-verb, with nothing to lift. Job said it at his losses (cf. Job 1:21) and Paul repeats it (cf. 1 Timothy 6:7); the Preacher states it as cold accounting.

16.text: And this too is a sickening evil: exactly as he came, so shall he go, and what profit does he have who has toiled for the wind?
16.amp: And this also is a sore [chalah] evil [ra], that in all points as he came [bo], so shall he go [yalak]: and what profit [yithron] has he that has laboured [amal] for the wind [ruach]?
16.notes: yithron (H3504), the ledger-word, meets its bleakest entry: wages paid in ruach (H7307), wind. A man can spend forty years earning what cannot be gripped, banked, or bequeathed.

17.text: All his days he eats in darkness besides, with great vexation, sickness, and anger for company.
17.amp: All his days [yom] also he eats [akal] in darkness [choshek], and he has much [rabah] sorrow [kaas — vexation] and wrath [qetseph] with his sickness [choli].
17.notes: Eating in choshek (H2822), darkness: the miser's supper, alone, late, joyless, guarding the lamp-oil too. kaas (H3707), qetseph (H7110), and choli (H2483) — vexation, anger, and sickness — are the three companions his riches seated at the table.

18.text: Look at what I have seen: it is good and fitting for a man to eat and to drink and to find good in all his toil under the sun through the numbered days of the life God has given him, for this is his portion.
18.amp: Behold that which I have seen [raah]: it is good [tov] and comely [yapheh — fitting, beautiful] for one to eat [akal] and to drink [shatah], and to enjoy the good [tov] of all his labour [amal] that he takes under the sun all the days [yom] of his life [chay], which God [Elohim] gives [natan] him: for it is his portion [cheleq].
18.notes: yapheh (H3303), fitting and beautiful, the word from 3:11: received rightly, the ordinary table is one of the things God has made beautiful in its time. cheleq (H2506), the portion again — and the days themselves are counted out ('the number of the days', the KJV margin) by the same giving hand.

19.text: Moreover, when God gives any man riches and wealth, and gives him with them the power to eat of it, to take up his portion, and to rejoice in his toil, this is the gift of God.
19.amp: Every man [adam] also to whom God [Elohim] has given [natan] riches and wealth [nekes], and has given him power to eat [akal] thereof, and to take [nasa] his portion [cheleq], and to rejoice [samach] in his labour [amal]; this is the gift [mattath] of God.
19.notes: The crucial second giving: wealth and the power to enjoy it are separate grants, and verse 13's hoarder proves they can come apart. mattath (H4991), the gift-word from 3:13 — natan (H5414) sounds three times, because everything in the verse descends from the same hand.

20.text: For such a man will not brood over the days of his life, because God keeps him answered and occupied with the joy of his heart.
20.amp: For he shall not much [rabah] remember [zakar — brood over] the days [yom] of his life [chay]; because God [Elohim] answers [anah — keeps him occupied] him in the joy [simchah] of his heart [leb].
20.notes: anah (H6031) here carries the sense of keeping occupied or answered: God so fills the man's present with simchah (H8057) that the vapor-questions lose their grip on him. The cure for brooding over life is not an argument but a gladness.
